source.name: BBC Science & Environment
source.title: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time
source.summary: The rocket stage was caught mid air using huge mechanical arms nicknamed “chopsticks”.
source.evidence_text:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket for the first time, after a flight lasting twenty-two and a half hours.
The Ship completed 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower.
The rocket returned to Earth and hovered near its launch tower whose mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - then secured it.
There were loud cheers from SpaceX staff who were watching the flight as the rocket returned to the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas.
The company had hoped to catch the bottom part of the rocket as well, but this was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday.
But the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.
SpaceX needs to reliably recover both parts of Starship so that it can fly repeatedly and drastically reduce costs.
The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.
The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.
This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable.
SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.
Any problems would have resulted in the ship being brought down in the ocean in the same way as the booster.
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket would take spaceflight to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society - but it didn't happen this time.
"Not recovering the first stage is a setback. But they have recovered Super Heavy before and so successfully returning and recovering the Ship, is a substantial step forward. They have demonstrated the two halves of the recovery challenge, just not yet on the same flight. The next milestone would be stitching those achievements together and then proving they can do it reliably, repeatedly and economically."
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

vocabulary.definition: A cancellation of a planned operation triggered by a control system rather than a direct human decision.
Changing course towards an alternative destination instead of continuing along the intended route.
A group of satellites organised to operate together as a system.
Dependent on a particular condition being satisfied before something can proceed.
An important goal maintained over an extended period, without implying that it has been achieved.
A significant achievement that marks progress towards a larger objective.
In a way that keeps costs low enough for an activity to be financially practical.
Possible consequences or wider effects that a development has for another undertaking.
Arrange or adapt a vehicle’s design and equipment so that it can perform a particular function.
Responsibilities or promised undertakings that an organisation is expected to fulfil.

grammar.explanation: To express an unreal past condition in a formal register, place “had” before the subject and omit “if”. Use “would have” plus a past participle for the imagined consequence; here, the condition concerns problems emerging before recovery.
grammar.example_quote: Had problems emerged, the Ship would have been brought down in the ocean instead.

quiz.question: Which assessment best captures the significance and limitation of this flight?

It established an upper-stage recovery achievement, while recovery of both sections on one flight remained unproven.
It repeated an established upper-stage recovery procedure but introduced a new booster recovery method.
option_feedback: The upper stage was recovered, but the booster exploded, so combined recovery was not demonstrated.
The upper-stage capture was a first, whereas combining the two recovery achievements remained a future milestone.
The upper-stage capture was new; the booster had already been caught on three earlier tests.

quiz.question: What does the account establish about the booster’s departure from its intended recovery sequence?
options: Its own control systems initiated a cancellation before it headed towards the ocean.
A decision made after the ocean explosion cancelled its planned return.
It completed the planned tower recovery before being redirected towards the ocean.
option_feedback: The automated abort preceded the diversion, hovering and explosion.
The cancellation occurred before the booster diverted and exploded, rather than afterwards.
The booster diverted to the ocean and exploded; the tower recovery concerned the upper stage.

quiz.question: What does “contingent on” convey about the proposed upper-stage recovery?
options: The assessment would explain the recovery after it had already occurred.
The assessment was an additional task that could not affect the recovery decision.
Proceeding with the recovery effort depended on the assessment.
option_feedback: “Contingent on” expresses a prerequisite, rather than a retrospective explanation.
The phrase makes the assessment relevant to whether the recovery effort would proceed.
“Contingent on” establishes a condition; it does not present the recovery effort as unconditional.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the same inverted past counterfactual pattern to imagine a combined recovery that did not occur on this flight?

Had both sections been recovered together, the flight would have demonstrated combined recovery.
Should both sections be recovered together, the flight will demonstrate combined recovery.
option_feedback: “Were both sections recovered” introduces a hypothetical condition, but it does not use the requested “had” plus past participle pattern.
“Had both sections been recovered” inverts a past perfect condition, and “would have demonstrated” supplies the imagined past consequence.
“Should both sections be recovered” presents an open possibility rather than the requested past counterfactual.

Its operating history establishes that recovering an entire Starship will necessarily be affordable.
Its lower-stage reuse provides an example of recovery contributing to lower launch costs.

Falcon 9 provides supporting experience, but the reading does not guarantee Starship’s future operating costs.
The reading explicitly connects reuse of Falcon 9’s lower section with substantial launch-cost reductions.

quiz.question: In Macdonald’s assessment, what would constitute the next “milestone”?
options: Combining the separate recovery achievements and establishing dependable, financially practical repetition.
Repeating the upper-stage capture while leaving combined recovery for a later development programme.
Increasing satellite deployment before evaluating whether either rocket section can be recovered.
option_feedback: His assessment connects combined recovery with demonstrating repeated operation at a practical cost.
Another upper-stage capture alone would not satisfy the stated goal of combining the two achievements.
The milestone concerns recovery and its repeatability, rather than the number of satellites deployed.

quiz.question: What additional requirement does “economically” introduce alongside repeated recovery?
options: The recovery process must occur more frequently than Falcon 9 launches.
The recovery process must be financially practical as well as technically repeatable.
The recovery process must eliminate every expense associated with launching.
option_feedback: “Economically” concerns cost, and the reading sets no requirement to exceed Falcon 9’s launch frequency.
The word adds a financial standard to the technical requirement of repeated successful recovery.
“Economically” means financially practical; it does not mean entirely free of expense.

quiz.question: Which conclusion about the proposed 2028 Moon landing is supported?
options: The upper-stage capture confirms that the landing timetable will be met.
The booster’s loss establishes that the landing timetable has been abandoned.
Starship’s progress matters to the timetable, but this achievement does not guarantee it.
